title: Memory-Induced Limits on Entanglement Distribution
authors: Roberto Benjamin Salazar Vargas, Hayden Zammit, Trevor Spiteri, Gianluca Valentino, Tony J. G. Apollaro, Johann A. Briffa
abstract: We investigate the operational limits of entanglement distribution through quantum channels reused without reinitialization. Building on an effective repeated-use channel description, we show that residual excitations left in the channel from previous uses act as a memory source that progressively suppresses coherent quantum transmission. To quantify this limitation, we derive an analytical lower bound on the quantum capacity and combine it with the Holevo-Werner semidefinite-programming upper bound. We also provide an analytical criterion to identify entanglement-breaking channels, with thresholds that depend jointly on chain length and reuse. For perfect-state-transfer chains, the resulting capacity window yields tighter estimates than previous bounds, with the relative improvement becoming substantially more pronounced closer to the entanglement-breaking threshold. Moreover, on the second use, our lower bound certifies a maximal relative timing-error tolerance across all chains with internal memory that lies just below 22.63% and is attained by the three-site chain. We further derive a fundamental relative timing-error threshold of 36.41%, above which we analytically guarantee zero unassisted quantum capacity for every chain with internal memory, independent of the number of uses. These results establish a clear benchmark model for repeated entanglement distribution, and identify timing precision, chain length, and memory accumulation as fundamental constraints on scalable quantum-network architectures.
summary: This work analyzes how reusing a quantum channel without resetting it causes memory-induced degradation, suppressing entanglement transmission. By deriving tight lower and upper bounds on quantum capacity, the authors establish fundamental limits based on timing precision and chain length. These results provide a crucial benchmark for designing robust, scalable quantum communication networks.
main_problem: The paper investigates the operational limits of distributing entanglement through quantum channels that are repeatedly used without being fully reinitialized.
main_result: It establishes fundamental thresholds for entanglement distribution, notably a 36.41% relative timing-error threshold guaranteeing zero unassisted quantum capacity for any chain with internal memory.
method: The authors derive analytical lower bounds on quantum capacity and combine them with the Holevo-Werner semidefinite-programming upper bound to characterize the achievable rate.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum state transfer through a spin-1/2 chain of N sites, where the internal sites act as a memory source that accumulates residual excitations upon channel reuse.
key_observables: Quantum capacity, residual excitations, relative timing error, and the quantum capacity window.
important_parameters: Chain length (N), number of uses, and the relative timing error ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis contrasts the standard assumption of a fully reset (memoryless) channel with the case of channel reuse retaining internal memory.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes reference Figure 1 illustrating the protocol for transferring quantum information via repeated use of the same channel.
paper_structure: The paper develops an effective repeated-use channel description, derives multiple bounds (lower bound, Holevo-Werner upper bound), and analyzes the capacity window, culminating in the derivation of fundamental error thresholds.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative framework for understanding decoherence and resource limitations in scalable quantum network architectures, directly impacting the feasibility of quantum repeaters.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Protocol for transferring quantum information from an n-qubit sender register (red spheres) to an n-qubit receiver register (blue spheres) through repeated use of the same quantum channel (green spheres). The ith transfer occurs at time ti.

FIG. 2: Analytical lower bound LB(n), bottleneck bound BN(n), and Holevo–Werner upper bounds HW(n, l) as functions of the channel-use number n for chain length N = 10 at relative readout timing errors δ ∈{1%, 10%, 16%}.

FIG. 3: Analytical lower bound LB(n) across channel use number n and chain length N for relative readout timing errors δ ∈{10%, 16%, 22%}. The red line indicates the entanglement-breaking threshold nEB (the hatched region corresponds to n ≥nEB), and the blue line marks the critical chain length NC, at or above which γ(N)(δ) ≥1/2.

FIG. 4: Bottleneck upper bound BN(n) across channel-use number n and chain length N for relative readout timing errors δ ∈{10%, 16%, 22%}. The red staircase marks the entanglement-breaking boundary nEB(N, δ), with n ≥nEB hatched. The blue dashed line marks the critical chain length NC, at or above which γ(N)(δ) ≥1/2 and BN(n) = 0 for every n.

FIG. 5: Holevo–Werner SDP upper bound HW(n, l = 10) across channel-use number n and chain length N for relative readout timing errors δ ∈{10%, 16%, 22%}. The red staircase marks the entanglement-breaking boundary nEB(N, δ), while the blue dashed line marks the critical length NC, at or above which γ(N)(δ) ≥1/2. Hatched cells satisfy n ≥nEB and therefore belong to a zero-capacity region.
